missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to describe the difference between longitudinal and transverse waves.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson defines only longitudinal waves (keyPoints[0].content: "The particles oscillate parallel to the direction of travel"). It never defines a transverse wave (oscillations perpendicular to the direction of travel), so the student cannot describe the difference. The word 'transverse' appears only as a wrong option in checkpoint 0.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The ripples on a water surface are an example of a transverse wave.
missing_spec_content.why: Water ripples are not mentioned anywhere in the lesson.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to describe evidence that, for both ripples on a water surface and sound waves in air, it is the wave and not the water or air itself that travels.
missing_spec_content.why: keyPoints[0].tutor_note states "The molecules themselves don't travel along with the wave" but gives no evidence. Examples would be a floating object bobbing in place on ripples, or a sound reaching you while the air does not flow towards you. Ripples are not covered at all.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Sound waves can travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson covers the speed of sound in solids. It does not teach that sound waves cause vibrations in solids or that these disturbances are converted between sound waves and vibrations of solids.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate which causes the sensation of sound.
missing_spec_content.why: The ear drum and the mechanism of hearing are not mentioned, even though the lesson is titled "Sound waves and hearing".

missing_spec_content.spec_text: describe, with examples, processes which convert wave disturbances between sound waves and vibrations in solids. Examples may include the effect of sound waves on the ear drum
missing_spec_content.why: No examples of converting between sound waves and vibrations in solids are taught. A speaker cone is mentioned only as a source of sound, not as a conversion process.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works over a limited frequency range. This restricts the limits of human hearing. ... explain why such processes only work over a limited frequency range and the relevance of this to human hearing.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson states the 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz range but never explains why hearing is limited. It does not teach that the ear drum and other parts can only vibrate effectively over a limited frequency range.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to explain in qualitative terms, how the differences in velocity, absorption and reflection between different types of wave in solids and liquids can be used both for detection and exploration of structures which are hidden from direct observation.
missing_spec_content.why: Absorption is not mentioned. Differences between types of wave in solids and liquids are not used to explain detection or exploration.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Ultrasound waves are partially reflected when they meet a boundary between two different media.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never says the reflection is partial. That some ultrasound is transmitted is what allows deeper boundaries to be imaged.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: This allows ultrasound waves to be used for both medical and industrial imaging.
missing_spec_content.why: Industrial imaging (for example, detecting flaws in materials) is not taught. The lesson gives "industrial cleaning" instead (keyPoints[3].content), which is a different application.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Seismic waves are produced by earthquakes. P-waves are longitudinal, seismic waves. P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids. S-waves are transverse, seismic waves. S-waves cannot travel through a liquid. P-waves and S-waves provide evidence for the structure and size of the Earth's core.
missing_spec_content.why: Seismic waves, P-waves, S-waves and the evidence they give for the Earth's core are not covered at all.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be aware that the study of seismic waves provided new evidence that led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable.

above_gcse.text: Below 20 Hz: infrasound. It is too low to hear. Earthquakes and whales make it.
above_gcse.why: Infrasound is not in the specification sections. It is also given as a key term and revision card bullet, which could suggest it is examinable.

above_gcse.text: Loudness is measured indirectly in decibels (dB).
above_gcse.why: Decibels are not in the specification sections.

above_gcse.text: These limits change with age. Older adults often cannot hear above 15,000–17,000 Hz.
above_gcse.why: Not required. The specification only requires the range 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

above_gcse.text: Sound can be reflected (echoes), refracted and diffracted, just like other waves.
above_gcse.why: Diffraction is not in these specification sections and is not otherwise required for sound at this level.
The specification does not require students to recall the speed of sound in particular media.

above_gcse.text: industrial cleaning: high-frequency vibrations shake dirt loose.
above_gcse.why: Not in the specification, which asks for industrial imaging. It may lead the student to give the wrong industrial use in an exam.

factual_errors.text: ~340 m/s in air at room temperature; faster in denser media
factual_errors.correction: The speed of sound is not set by density alone. It depends mainly on how stiff (incompressible) the medium is. Denser materials can carry sound more slowly: lead is denser than steel but sound travels more slowly in it, and sound is slower in denser gases. Safer wording is 'generally fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases'.

factual_errors.text: Light slows down in denser media, but sound speeds up.
factual_errors.correction: Stated as a general rule, this is incorrect for sound. Sound speed depends mainly on stiffness, not density (see above).

factual_errors.text: ultrasound pulses reflect off boundaries between tissues, such as between a baby and the fluid around it. The reflected pulses are used to build up an image.
factual_errors.correction: Ultrasound waves are only partially reflected at a boundary between two different media. The rest is transmitted, which is why reflections from deeper boundaries can also be detected.

factual_errors.text: It is safe, and it reflects off boundaries inside the body.
factual_errors.correction: Ultrasound is partially reflected at boundaries between different media.

wrong_terms.text: sonar: ships send ultrasound pulses toward the seabed. They time the returning echo to measure the water depth.
industrial cleaning: high-frequency vibrations shake dirt loose.

checkpoint_mismatch.checkpoint: 1: "A sound wave's frequency is increased, but its amplitude stays the same. How does this change the sound you hear?"
checkpoint_mismatch.key_point: keyPoints[1].heading: "Speed of sound in different media"
checkpoint_mismatch.why: Checkpoint 1 tests frequency, pitch and loudness, which are taught in keyPoints[2] ("Frequency, amplitude, pitch, and loudness"). keyPoints[1] does not teach pitch or loudness, so it does not support the answer. Its own content on speed of sound is untested, and there is no checkpoint 2 for keyPoints[2].

not_checked: All keyPoints have "diagram": null, so there were no diagrams or images to check.
The checkpoint review assumes each checkpoint key ("0", "1", "3") refers to the keyPoints entry with the same index. Key "2" is absent.
